samples.summary: Roll-up still discloses per-document metrics for documents the caller is not allowed to open in detail
samples.evidence: The change formalizes that per-document analytics is manager-only (`GET /documents/:id/analytics` throws Forbidden at analytics.controller.ts:170-174), and resolves the mismatch in the UI direction only: `workspaceDashboard` (member-gated via `assertMember`, line 222) keeps returning a `byDocument` row containing `title`, `views` and `uniqueVisitors` for every document in the workspace, and merely marks `canManage: false` (lines 240-251) so the frontend hides the 'Details' link (workspace-analytics.tsx:92). Attack: any plain workspace member calls `GET /workspaces/:wid/analytics` directly (no UI needed) and reads view/unique-visitor counts, plus — via the new `canManage` flag — which documents were authored by someone else, for documents whose detail dashboard the server deliberately refuses them. This is a partial information-disclosure inconsistency between the two tiers rather than a bypass of the detail gate; the exposure of counts pre-dates this change, the `canManage` authorship signal is new (though the documents list already exposes an equivalent flag).

samples.summary: Hand-rolled SQL quoting for StarRocks escapes only single quotes, not backslashes
samples.evidence: `sql()` (analytics-warehouse.service.ts:33-35) builds every warehouse predicate by string interpolation (`buildQueries` line 89, `buildWorkspaceQueries` line 152; the `byDocument` query feeding the `documentRows` mapper touched by this diff at line 226) and escapes only `'` by doubling. StarRocks speaks the MySQL protocol, where a trailing backslash in a literal escapes the closing quote (`'a\'` swallows the delimiter), so a value ending in `\` would let the remainder of the string continue the SQL expression — e.g. `... document_id = 'x\' AND 1=1 OR '` — reading arbitrary `view_events` rows across workspaces. I could not complete the vector: the only strings reaching `sql()` are `day()` output (derived from `Date`, safe) and document ids, and ids are server-generated UUIDs (`prisma/schema.prisma:42 id String @default(uuid())`) that must round-trip a `findUnique`/`findMany` before being interpolated, so no attacker-controlled string currently reaches the quoter. Reported as a defense-in-depth gap on the escaping helper; it is pre-existing code, not added by this diff.
searchedFor: grep isDocumentManager / getDocumentAnalytics / getWorkspaceAnalytics call sites
prisma schema Document model id default

verdict.reason: Verified the code exists exactly as described. `sql()` at analytics-warehouse.service.ts:33-35 escapes only single quotes (`value.replace(/'/g, "''")`) and leaves backslashes untouched, while its own comment (line 32) declares it the sole injection control because StarRocks has no prepared statements. Every predicate is built by string interpolation (line 89 `where`, lines 91-100; line 149 `documentIds.map(sql)` into the `IN (...)` list at line 152, feeding byDocument at line 157 -> documentRows at 223-233), and execution is fully raw via `this.pool!.query(query)` (lines 197, 202, 209, 217, 224) with no placeholder array, so mysql2 adds no escaping. StarRocks uses MySQL-protocol literal semantics where a trailing backslash consumes the closing quote, so the escaper is genuinely incomplete for its dialect. On reachability I reached the same place the reviewer did: analytics.controller.ts:163-166 requires the id to resolve via findUnique before line 177 passes the raw route param in, ids are DB-generated (schema.prisma:42 `@default(uuid())`) and no create path (document.service.ts:82, document.controller.ts:132/214, api/v1/documents.controller.ts:54, api/v1/files.controller.ts:111) accepts a client-supplied id. But that is a data-provenance invariant, not a guard: no call site validates the format of documentId before interpolation, and the workspace path feeds stored ids straight through, so `already-guarded` does not apply. Under this lens's severity rubric, "a clear security weakness that isn't yet a full exploit" is major, so incomplete exploitability is not a basis to drop it. Broken escaping in a hand-rolled SQL quoter is in the injection lane, so `out-of-scope` does not apply either.
